newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government attacks race row politician.
newsitem.headline: Australian government attacks race row politician.

text.p: Australia's conservative government, stung by race row politician Pauline Hanson's surging popularity, on Thursday attacked the controversial independent as divisive, absurd and a threat to prosperity.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer and Trade Minister Tim Fischer said Hanson's views could also harm Australia's position in Asia -- its economic lifeline for the next century.
Downer said Hanson's views were of "a little Australia, inward-looking, narrow-minded, protectionist and disconnected from our own neighbourhood".

"They are not the views of the Australian government. These are not the views of the vast majority of the Australian people," said Downer before he and Fischer attended talks with the heads of Canberra's regional diplomatic missions.
"Rather, they are views which create divisiveness within Australia and portray a false view of this country and of the true values which constitute and sustain our society," he said.

"They are views which, if adopted widely within this country, would harm our national prosperity and diminish the role Australia can and must play in Asia and, moreover, they would diminish Australia itself."
Downer said Hanson's stand of banning foreign investment and her racist immigration policy would cost tens of thousands of Australian jobs.
Fischer said Hanson threatened Australia's increasing income from trade with its booming Asian neighbours.

"Australia would be dumb to tear up its bread ticket for the next century by jeopardising its trade by the aspects of the Hanson agenda, which would do exactly that," Fischer told reporters after the diplomatic talks.
The stinging attack by the two ministers contrasts with Prime Minister John Howard's reluctance to criticise Hanson.
Howard has prefered to dimiss Hanson as a populist whose support would wither when Australians realise her policies are simplistic and unworkable.
Latest opinion polls show Hanson, who sparked a divisive naitonal race row last year, is rapdidly attracting an increasing number of voters disillusioned with major parties.
The level of support shown in the polls, now around 10 percent, would be enough to give Hanson's One Nation party a chance of an influential role in parliament under the right circumstances.
